name: Blink
funFact: Humans blink around 15–20 times per minute — so often that our eyes are closed for roughly 10% of our waking hours.

name: Heartbeat
funFact: The human heart beats about 100,000 times a day — over a lifetime, that's roughly 3 billion heartbeats.

name: Coffee break
funFact: The formal coffee break was introduced in 1902 by the Stoughton, Wisconsin city council — it's been legally protected in some workplaces ever since.

name: TV episode
funFact: The 45-minute TV drama format was designed around the commercial break structure of 1960s American broadcasting — and has barely changed since.

name: Song
funFact: The average pop song has gotten shorter since streaming — from 3m 50s in 2013 to under 3m 20s by 2020, partly because artists get paid per stream after 30 seconds.

name: Power nap
funFact: NASA research found that a 26-minute nap improved pilot performance by 34% and alertness by 100%.

name: Toilet scroll
description: Average phone session in the bathroom ≈ 8 minutes.
funFact: A study found 75% of people use their phone in the bathroom — and the average session is 8 minutes, longer than most news articles take to read.

name: Average commute
exampleMeme: The time you spend regretting your life choices.
funFact: The average commute in the US is 27.6 minutes — adding up to about 9 full days per year spent getting to and from work.

name: Work day
funFact: The 8-hour work day was championed by Robert Owen in 1817 with the slogan: 8 hours labour, 8 hours recreation, 8 hours rest.

name: Lunar month
funFact: Every calendar system in history has had to grapple with the fact that 12 lunar months is 11 days shorter than a solar year — solved differently by different cultures.

name: Week
funFact: The 7-day week has no astronomical basis — it was invented in ancient Mesopotamia around 600 BC and spread so universally that no culture has successfully replaced it.

name: Month
funFact: No month is exactly the same length — February's 28 days exist because Roman emperor Augustus stole a day from it to make his month (August) as long as Julius Caesar's July.

name: Year
funFact: A year is not exactly 365 days — it's 365.25 days, which is why we add a leap day every 4 years. Even then we over-correct, so century years skip the leap day unless divisible by 400.

name: Decade
exampleMeme: Long enough to regret a haircut.
funFact: Humans are notoriously bad at remembering when things happened within a decade — a phenomenon called 'telescoping', where distant events feel more recent than they are.

name: 100m sprint
funFact: Usain Bolt's world record 100m time of 9.58s means he averaged 37.6 km/h — his top speed mid-race was 44.7 km/h.

name: Mars day
funFact: A day on Mars (called a 'sol') is just 37 minutes longer than an Earth day — making Mars the most Earth-like planet in terms of day length.

name: Dog year
funFact: The '7 dog years per human year' rule is a myth — dogs age rapidly in their first 2 years, then slow down. A 1-year-old dog is more like a 15-year-old human.

name: Human lifespan
description: Average human lifespan ≈ 72 years ≈ 2.27 billion seconds.
funFact: If you're 30 years old, you've lived approximately 946,080,000 seconds — nearly a billion. You'll hit the billion-second mark at around 31 years and 8 months.

name: Since the dinosaurs
description: Time since non-avian dinosaur extinction ≈ 66 million years.
funFact: Birds are technically dinosaurs — the Velociraptor was more closely related to a modern pigeon than to a T-Rex. So dinosaurs didn't go extinct; they're outside your window.

name: Age of the universe
description: Age of the observable universe ≈ 13.8 billion years.
funFact: If the entire history of the universe were compressed into one calendar year, modern humans wouldn't appear until 11:59:59 PM on December 31st — the last second.

name: Light to the Moon
description: Time for light to travel Earth to Moon ≈ 1.28 s.
funFact: During the Apollo missions, the 1.28-second one-way delay meant every question from mission control waited 2.56 seconds for an answer — clearly audible in the recordings.

name: Gym session
exampleMeme: One session closer to being mysterious.

name: Bad meeting
exampleMeme: This could have been a message.

name: Camera shutter (fast)
description: Fast camera shutter speed ≈ 1/1000th of a second.
funFact: A hummingbird beats its wings 80 times per second — a 1/1000s shutter can freeze individual wingbeats. The world's fastest cameras can now capture one trillion frames per second, fast enough to film light itself travelling through a bottle.

name: Unskippable YouTube ad
exampleMeme: The universal unit of digital suffering.
funFact: YouTube introduced the 5-second skip button in 2010 after research showed users would leave the platform entirely rather than watch a full ad. The 5-second threshold was determined by user testing — any shorter and advertisers complained their brand wasn't registering.

name: Football half-time
funFact: The 15-minute half-time was formally standardised by FIFA in 1938. Premier League clubs generate more revenue from half-time advertising alone than many clubs' entire annual budgets in lower divisions.

name: Pregnancy
funFact: Human pregnancies are unusually long relative to body size compared to other mammals. Human babies are also born remarkably undeveloped — if born with the neurological maturity of a newborn chimp, gestation would need to be 21 months.

name: Voyager 1 travel time
description: Time since Voyager 1 launched ≈ 47 years (as of 2024).
funFact: Voyager 1 launched in 1977 and is now the furthest human-made object from Earth at over 24 billion km away. It still communicates with NASA, but signals take over 22 hours to arrive at the speed of light. It runs on 70 watts of power — less than a light bulb.

name: The Roman Empire
description: Duration of the Western Roman Empire ≈ 1,229 years.
funFact: Rome was founded in 753 BC and the Western Empire fell in 476 AD — 1,229 years. The Eastern Roman Empire (Byzantine) continued until 1453, meaning 'Rome' in some form lasted 2,206 years. For context, the United States is currently 248 years old.

name: Since the pyramids
description: Time since the Great Pyramid was built ≈ 4,500 years.
funFact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landings than to the building of the pyramids. The Great Pyramid was already 2,500 years old when Cleopatra was born in 69 BC — the same age difference as between us and ancient Rome.

name: Light across the Milky Way
description: Time for light to cross the Milky Way ≈ 100,000 years.
funFact: The Milky Way is so vast that light takes 100,000 years to cross it. Our solar system is 26,000 light-years from the centre — roughly halfway out on one of the spiral arms. We orbit the galaxy's centre once every 230 million years.

name: Planck time
exampleMeme: The smallest tick of the universe's clock.
funFact: The Planck time is the smallest meaningful unit of time in physics — below it, our understanding of time itself breaks down. There are more Planck times in one second than there are seconds since the Big Bang. It's not just small; it's the boundary of what 'time' means.

name: Jiffy
description: Physics jiffy ≈ 33.3 picoseconds (time for light to travel 1 cm).
funFact: In physics, a jiffy is the time it takes light to travel one centimetre — about 33.3 picoseconds. In computing, it's the time between system timer interrupts (typically 10 milliseconds). The casual 'I'll be there in a jiffy' is off by a factor of about 300 million.

name: Shake
funFact: A 'shake' is 10 nanoseconds — defined by nuclear physicists as roughly the time for one step of a nuclear chain reaction. The name comes from 'two shakes of a lamb's tail.' A nuclear bomb's entire detonation sequence happens in about 50-60 shakes.

name: Microwave minute
description: One microwave minute = 60 seconds (but feels like 300).
exampleMeme: The longest minute known to science.
funFact: A microwave minute is physically identical to a regular minute — 60 seconds — but psychologists have documented that people consistently perceive waiting in front of a microwave as 2-3 times longer than the same duration spent doing anything else. The effect is called 'temporal dilation under boredom' and it's measurably stronger when you can see a countdown timer.

name: Moment
funFact: In medieval timekeeping, a 'moment' was a precise unit equal to 90 seconds — 1/40th of an hour. Monks used it to schedule prayers throughout the day. When someone says 'just a moment,' they're accidentally referencing a 12th-century monastic schedule.

name: Traffic light cycle
description: Average full traffic light cycle ≈ 90 seconds.
exampleMeme: The universe's way of testing your patience.
funFact: The average driver spends about 2 weeks of their life waiting at red lights. Traffic engineers call the moment when you're too far to stop but too close to make the yellow a 'dilemma zone' — and intersections are specifically timed to minimise how often drivers enter it.

name: Pomodoro
funFact: The Pomodoro Technique was invented by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s using a tomato-shaped kitchen timer ('pomodoro' is Italian for tomato). The 25-minute interval was chosen because Cirillo found it was the longest period most people could sustain genuine focus without their mind wandering.

name: Microcentury
funFact: The microcentury was popularised by a professor who told students 'I will never give a lecture longer than a microcentury.' At 52 minutes and 35.76 seconds, it's surprisingly close to a standard university lecture slot — which may not be a coincidence.

name: Watch
funFact: Ships divide the 24-hour day into six watches of 4 hours each. The 'dog watch' (4-6 PM and 6-8 PM) is split into two 2-hour halves specifically so crew rotations shift daily — otherwise the same sailors would always get the worst overnight watch.

name: Sidereal day
description: One sidereal day = 23 hours 56 minutes 4 seconds.
exampleMeme: The day you didn't know you had.
funFact: A sidereal day is 3 minutes and 56 seconds shorter than a solar day because the Earth has to rotate slightly more than 360° to face the Sun again (since it's also orbiting). Over a year, those missing minutes add up to exactly one extra rotation — which is why there are 366 sidereal days but only 365 solar days.

name: Fortnight
funFact: The word comes from the Old English 'fēowertyne niht' — fourteen nights. It's one of the few medieval time units still in active daily use, primarily in Britain, Australia, and New Zealand, where wages are commonly paid fortnightly.

name: Galactic year
description: One galactic year ≈ 225–250 million Earth years.
exampleMeme: One lap around the Milky Way.
funFact: A galactic year is the time it takes our solar system to orbit the centre of the Milky Way once — roughly 230 million years. The Sun has completed about 20 galactic years since it formed. The dinosaurs went extinct about 0.3 galactic years ago. All of recorded human history is about 0.00002 galactic years.

name: Feature film
funFact: The Academy defines a feature film as any motion picture 40 minutes or longer — but the average Hollywood film has steadily crept from 95 minutes in the 1980s to over 130 minutes today. Marvel films average 148 minutes, which is why your bladder has opinions about the MCU.

name: Human generation
exampleMeme: The gap between you and your parents.
funFact: A generation was historically considered 25 years, but modern demographers put it closer to 27-29 years in developed countries as the average age of first parenthood rises. There have been roughly 7,500 human generations since Homo sapiens emerged — and you share DNA with every single one of them.
